topic.title: How Medieval Cities Handled Their Waste

script.full_text: Picture a medieval city: fifty thousand people packed inside stone walls, and not a single sewer. The most pressing question wasn't war or plague. It was simply, where does it all go? The answer was a grim economy. Households used cesspits dug beneath their homes. When they filled, the night-soil men, the gong farmers, emptied them by hand after dark and hauled the waste beyond the walls. It was dangerous, low-paid, and constant. When the system failed, waste ran into the same rivers people drank from, and the diseases that followed could empty a city faster than any siege. Every flush you take today traces back to these grim lessons. Modern sanitation was never a sudden invention. It was built, painfully, on centuries of getting it wrong.
